history.origin_body: Dhanana takes its name from its founder, Dhanna Jaat, who first settled this land. Over generations, the Ghanghas Jat clan became the dominant family of the village. As the population grew and farmers began working distant fields, satellite settlements — Jatai, Sukhpura, and Kuchpad — were established nearby.
history.sub_villages_body: Dhanana is administered as three sub-villages: Dhanana I, Dhanana II, and Dhanana III — each a part of the same roots.

migrations.title: The Long Journey
migrations.subtitle: Seven chapters across four millennia — from the Eurasian steppe to the fields of Dhanana.
migrations.era1_body: On the grasslands east of the Ural mountains, the Sintashta people raised fortified settlements, buried warriors with their horses, and built the earliest known spoked-wheel chariots. Many scholars trace the Indo-Iranian languages to these herders.
migrations.era2_body: Moving south with their herds, steppe families reached the walled oasis towns of the Oxus civilization. At Gonur Depe they met farmers, traders, and new gods — and the cultures began to mingle.
migrations.era3_body: Long before any newcomers arrived, the Ghaggar plain was home to Rakhigarhi — among the largest cities of the Harappan civilization, barely 40 km from where Dhanana stands today.
migrations.era4_body: As the great Indus cities faded, life carried on in smaller farming villages like Mitathal — a close neighbour of present-day Dhanana. Here, Late Harappan traditions slowly blended with new arrivals from the northwest.
migrations.era5_body: In the land between the Saraswati and Drishadvati rivers, Vedic clans grazed their cattle and composed the hymns of the Rigveda. Kurukshetra became the sacred heartland of this new world.
migrations.era6_body: Painted Grey Ware settlements spread across the doab. At Hastinapura, remembered as the capital of the Mahabharata's Kuru kings, legend and archaeology meet.
migrations.era7_body: Centuries later, on this same ancient plain, Dhanna Jaat founded the village that bears his name. The Ghanghas clan put down roots here — and the long journey of generations found its home.
migrations.teaser_sub: Trace four millennia of journeys on an interactive map — from the steppe to Dhanana.
migrations.disclaimer: This map is an artistic, simplified visualization. Migration routes, dates, and connections are debated and actively researched — archaeology, linguistics, and ancient DNA each tell partial stories. The site names are real; the paths drawn between them are illustrative, not literal.
